readings.title: Counting birds before drawing conclusions
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A group of neighbours counted birds in a public garden. One unusually quiet morning led to concern that local species were disappearing. The central difficulty was a conclusion based on one morning. Cold weather had changed where birds fed, and several volunteers had arrived later than on previous visits. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried weekly counts at the same hour. The group agreed on fixed observation points, recorded weather and trained newcomers to recognise the most common birds. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed numbers rose and fell with conditions. The longer record showed variation rather than a steady decline, though it also suggested some areas offered less food. In response, the group adopted a seasonal record with clear limits. Volunteers published their methods and asked a local specialist to explain what their counts could and could not demonstrate. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: repeated observations support careful claims. A single quiet visit can be worth recording, but it should not be mistaken for evidence of a lasting change. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in counting birds before drawing conclusions, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

options.D: uneven growth in nearby planting beds

readings.title: Mapping noise around a station
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents near a station disagreed about when traffic noise was worst. Some blamed morning buses, while others pointed to late deliveries. The central difficulty was different impressions of peak noise. People heard sound from different rooms and at different times, so their reports were sincere but difficult to compare. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried sound readings at agreed locations. Volunteers used one type of meter, noted the time and weather, and avoided measuring directly beside a single passing vehicle. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed late deliveries created a short sharp peak. Morning traffic was steady, but the highest readings occurred during a smaller number of evening unloading events. In response, the group adopted talks about delivery times and routes. The group shared its figures with businesses and discussed changes that would reduce disturbance without stopping necessary deliveries. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: measurement can clarify a disagreement. The readings did not invalidate anyone’s experience; they helped identify when and where a practical change might matter most. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in mapping noise around a station, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: A weather diary at the school gate
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An adult education centre invited learners to keep a local weather diary. Many expected it to be a simple list of sunny and rainy days. The central difficulty was inconsistent ways of describing weather. One learner wrote cool where another wrote warm, and recording times differed from morning to late evening. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried shared times and simple instruments. The group chose a regular observation hour, used a thermometer in one shaded place and kept personal comments separate. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed consistent timing made patterns easier to see. After a month, learners could compare temperature changes without confusing them with measurements taken at different hours. In response, the group adopted a diary combining numbers and descriptions. The final pages showed measured values alongside notes about how wind or rain affected people’s plans. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: good records need agreed methods and context. Numbers became more useful when everyone knew how they were collected and could connect them to daily experience. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in a weather diary at the school gate, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: What soil samples can tell gardeners
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Several community gardeners noticed weak growth in one row of beds. They initially blamed the quality of the seeds. The central difficulty was uneven growth in nearby planting beds. The same seeds had grown well elsewhere, and one part of the site stayed wet long after rain. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried soil checks at several depths. A trained adviser showed volunteers how to take comparable samples and record drainage without disturbing all the plants. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed poor drainage explained the weakest area. The results did not prove that every plant problem had the same cause, but they pointed to a practical first change. In response, the group adopted a drainage improvement in one test bed. The group altered a small area and compared new growth before spending money on work across the entire site. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: small comparisons prevent costly assumptions. By checking soil before replacing seeds, gardeners learned which intervention deserved a careful trial. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in what soil samples can tell gardeners, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
People sometimes draw a strong conclusion from a single observation. A group of neighbours saw few birds in a garden one cold morning and worried that local species were disappearing. They decided to count birds every week at the same hour and to record the weather. The longer record showed numbers rising and falling with conditions. It did not prove that the environment was unchanged, but it gave the group a better basis for asking questions. Volunteers also invited a specialist to explain what their counts could show. Careful science includes repeated observations and an honest account of what remains uncertain.
translation.explanation: 注意but表示的转折与what引导的宾语从句。
translation.referenceAnswer: 人们有时会根据一次观察得出很强的结论。一群邻居在某个寒冷的早晨发现花园里鸟很少，担心当地鸟类正在消失。他们决定每周同一时间数鸟，并记录天气。较长时期的记录表明，数量会随条件变化。这并不能证明环境没有改变，却为团队提出问题提供了更好的依据。志愿者还请专家解释计数结果能说明什么。严谨的科学包括反复观察，也包括诚实说明尚不确定的部分。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a science club proposing a careful bird-counting project in a public garden. Explain how volunteers should record observations and why one morning is not enough for a conclusion.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖固定观察方法、记录条件与审慎结论。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Club Members,
I suggest a weekly bird count in the public garden from early spring to late summer. Volunteers should use the same observation points and begin at the same hour each week. We could provide a short guide to common local birds and ask new members to count with an experienced partner at first. The record sheet should include weather, time and any unusual disturbance near the garden.
One quiet morning should not make us claim that a species has disappeared. Birds may move because of cold weather or temporary food changes. After several months, we could compare the counts and ask a local specialist to help us interpret uncertain patterns. Publishing our method alongside the results would let other residents understand what our observations can and cannot show.
Yours sincerely,
A volunteer
